p.src: Now Marshal Xing Zheng crossed weapons with Guan Sheng. Before they had fought fifteen bouts, Guan Sheng raised his blade and cut him down from his horse. Seeing Xing Zheng slain, Huyan Zhuo drove his troops forward in a sweeping charge, and the six commandants fled south. Privy Councillor Lü, seeing the troops under his command utterly defeated, abandoned Dantu County and led the battered survivors toward Changzhou Prefecture. The ten Song generals seized the county offices and sent news of the victory to Vanguard Song, who brought the main army forward and encamped in Dantu County. He rewarded the entire army, urgently reported the victory to Pacification Commissioner Zhang, and moved troops to garrison Runzhou. The next day, Staff Officers Cong and Geng of headquarters brought rewards to Dantu County. Song Jiang respectfully received them and distributed them among the generals.

I shall now divide the troops and generals with you and advance by two routes. We will write the two destinations on lots and draw them before Heaven; whichever place each of us draws, there he shall lead his troops.” Song Jiang drew Changzhou and Suzhou, while Lu Junyi drew Xuanzhou and Huzhou. p.src: Now Lü Shinang, accompanied by six commanding officers, withdrew to Piling Prefecture in Changzhou and fortified it. Changzhou was already defended by the commanding officer Qian Zhenpeng, who had two deputy generals under him: one was Jin Jie, a native of Shanghao in Jinling County; the other was Xu Ding, one of Qian Zhenpeng's trusted confidants. Qian Zhenpeng had begun as a constable in Qingxi County. After assisting Fang La and repeatedly capturing cities, he had been promoted to Pacification Commissioner of Changzhou. When he heard that Privy Councillor Lü had been defeated, lost Runzhou, and retreated all the way to Changzhou, he immediately took Jin Jie and Xu Ding to open the gates and welcome him. After receiving him at the prefectural offices and offering him hospitality, they discussed how to meet the enemy. Qian Zhenpeng said, “Set your mind at ease, my lord. Though I am a man of little ability, I am willing to serve with the devotion of a dog or horse. I shall crush that scoundrel Song Jiang and his men, drive them back across the river, and recover Runzhou; only then will my wish be fulfilled!” Privy Councillor Lü reassured him, saying, “With a commissioner applying himself so earnestly, why should we fear that the realm will not be secured? Once success is achieved, I shall strongly recommend you to the throne for high promotion and a distinguished title.” A banquet was held that day, but there is no need to dwell upon it.

p.src: Meanwhile, Vanguard Song led the troops assigned to attack Changzhou and Suzhou, sending the cavalry forward at full speed toward Piling Prefecture. The chief general was Guan Sheng, commanding ten officers. Those ten were Qin Ming, Xu Ning, Huang Xin, Sun Li, Hao Siwen, Xuan Zan, Han Tao, Peng Qi, Ma Lin, and Yan Shun. The principal and deputy officers numbered eleven in all. Leading three thousand cavalry, they advanced straight to the walls of Changzhou, where they waved their banners, beat their drums, and challenged the defenders to battle. After observing them, Privy Councillor Lü asked, “Who dares go and drive back the enemy?” Qian Zhenpeng had his warhorse prepared and said, “I shall go forward and render service.” Privy Councillor Lü immediately assigned the six commanding officers to assist him. Who were the six? Ying Ming, Zhang Jinren, Zhao Yi, Shen Bian, Gao Keli, and Fan Chou. The seven generals led five thousand troops out through the opened city gates and across the lowered drawbridge. Wielding a Wind-Sweeping Saber and riding a curly-maned Red Hare horse, Qian Zhenpeng was the first out of the city.

p.src: When Guan Sheng saw them, he drew his troops back a short distance, allowing Qian Zhenpeng to form his battle line, with the six commanding officers divided between his two wings. Facing the enemy, Guan Sheng halted his horse at the front, laid his saber crosswise, and shouted sternly, “Listen, you rebels! You have aided one common man in rebellion and brought ruin upon innocent lives, provoking the wrath of gods and men alike! Today the armies of Heaven have reached your borders, yet still unaware of your impending deaths, you dare come out to resist us! We swear not to withdraw until every last one of you brigands has been put to death!” Qian Zhenpeng flew into a rage at this and cursed him: “You are nothing but a band of brigands from Liangshan Marsh, ignorant of Heaven's appointed time! Instead of aspiring to establish a royal dominion, you surrendered to a benighted and immoral emperor and now come to contend with our great realm. Today I shall not stop until I have slaughtered you so utterly that not a scrap of armor returns!” Guan Sheng was enraged. Brandishing his Green Dragon Crescent Blade, he charged straight at him; Qian Zhenpeng swung his Wind-Sweeping Saber and rushed forward to meet him. The two generals fought for more than thirty bouts, until Qian Zhenpeng gradually weakened and could no longer withstand his opponent. Under the southern army's standard, two commanding officers saw Qian Zhenpeng faltering. Leveling their spears, both spurred out together to attack Guan Sheng from either side. Zhao Yi came at Guan Sheng from the upper side and Fan Chou from the lower. Under the Song army's standard, this provoked two deputy generals. One brandished a Sword of Mourning, the other wielded a Tiger-Eye Whip, and both galloped out: they were Huang Xin, Guardian of the Three Mountains, and Sun Li, the Sick Yuchi. Thus six generals, paired into three contests, fought before the battle lines. Privy Councillor Lü urgently ordered Xu Ding and Jin Jie out of the city to assist in the battle. Receiving the order, the two generals took up their weapons, mounted their horses, and rode straight to the front. There they saw Zhao Yi fighting Huang Xin and Fan Chou fighting Sun Li, each pair evenly matched. As the fighting grew intense, Zhao Yi and Fan Chou gradually lost the advantage; Xu Ding and Jin Jie each wielded a great saber and rode out from the formation. From the Song formation, the two generals Han Tao and Peng Qi rode out together to meet them. Jin Jie engaged Han Tao, while Xu Ding engaged Peng Qi. With those four generals joining the struggle, five pairs were now fighting before the lines.

p.src: Now Jin Jie had long harbored the wish to surrender to the Great Song. Intending to throw his own ranks into disorder, he deliberately fought only a few bouts before wheeling his horse and fleeing first toward his formation; Han Tao seized the opportunity and pursued him. In the southern formation, Gao Keli saw Han Tao pressing Jin Jie hard. Taking up his carved bow, he nocked a stout arrow and drew the string to its full extent. The arrow whistled through the air, struck Han Tao in the cheek, and sent him tumbling backward from his horse. Qin Ming immediately slapped his horse forward and came swinging his wolf-toothed mace to the rescue, but Zhang Jinren had already dashed out from the other side and thrust a spear into Han Tao's throat, ending his life. Peng Qi and Han Tao had served as paired senior and deputy officers and were as close as brothers. Seeing Han Tao dead, Peng Qi was desperate to avenge him. He broke away from Xu Ding and charged toward the enemy formation in search of Gao Keli. Xu Ding pursued him, but Qin Ming intercepted Xu Ding and engaged him in combat. p.src: Privy Councillor Lü was deeply troubled by Qian Zhenpeng’s defeat. He dispatched three urgent messages in succession to the Third Prince Fang Mao at Suzhou, begging for reinforcements, while also drafting a memorial to the imperial court. Then came another report: “Five hundred infantrymen are attacking the city. Their banner identifies their leader as Li Kui, the Black Whirlwind.” Privy Councillor Lü said, “That brute is the fiercest outlaw of Liangshan Marsh, a warrior well accustomed to killing. Who dares go first and seize him for me?” Two victorious commanders who had distinguished themselves, Gao Keli and Zhang Jinren, stepped forward from before the command tent. Privy Councillor Lü said, “If you two capture this bandit, I shall personally recommend you for promotion and reward you handsomely.” Commanders Zhang and Gao each snatched up a spear, mounted his horse, and led a thousand cavalry and infantry out of the city to meet the enemy. At the sight of them, Li Kui the Black Whirlwind drew his five hundred infantrymen into a single line, gripped a broad-bladed axe in each hand, and stood before the formation; Bao Xu, the God of Death, stood beside him wielding a great broad-bladed sword; Xiang Chong and Li Gun each held a barbarian shield in his left hand and an iron javelin in his right. All four wore iron armor protecting chest and back and took their places at the front of the formation. The two commanders Gao and Zhang were truly victorious wildcats imagining themselves fiercer than tigers, crows emboldened by circumstance to harry an eagle. They drew up their thousand troops close beneath the city walls.

p.src: Among the Song troops were several scouts who recognized Gao Keli and Zhang Jinren as the men who had killed Han Tao and Peng Qi. They pointed them out to the Black Whirlwind and said, “Those two leading the troops are the very men who killed our Generals Han and Peng!” Hearing this, Li Kui said not a word. He raised his two broad-bladed axes and charged straight across to the opposing formation. Seeing Li Kui charge into the opposing ranks, Bao Xu quickly called to Xiang Chong and Li Gun to whirl their barbarian shields and hurry forward in support. All four gave a great shout together and rolled headlong into the enemy formation. Gao Keli and Zhang Jinren were taken completely by surprise. Before they could respond, they tried desperately to wheel their horses, but the two barbarian shields had already rolled beneath the animals’ jaws. When Gao Keli and Zhang Jinren thrust their spears downward from horseback, Xiang Chong and Li Gun met them with their shields. Li Kui’s axe flashed and hacked down Gao Keli’s horse by the legs, pitching Gao Keli from the saddle. Xiang Chong cried, “Take him alive!” But Li Kui was a man who delighted in killing; how could he restrain himself? His axe had already fallen and struck off Gao Keli’s head. Bao Xu dragged Zhang Jinren down from his horse and likewise cut off his head with one stroke. The four of them slaughtered wildly through the enemy ranks. The Black Whirlwind tied Gao Keli’s head at his waist and swung his two broad-bladed axes, heedless of heaven or earth, hewing a path through the enemy. He drove the thousand cavalry and infantry back into the city, killing three or four hundred of them, and pursued them all the way to the drawbridge. Li Kui and Bao Xu were intent on fighting their way into the city, but Xiang Chong and Li Gun held them back with all their strength. Logs and stones were already crashing down from the walls. The four returned to the front of their formation, where the five hundred soldiers stood drawn up in their original single line, not daring to move rashly. They had originally intended to join the melee, but feared that the Black Whirlwind, unable to distinguish friend from foe, would cut down anyone he saw; for that reason they dared not approach.

p.src: As dust billowed in the distance, the forces of Vanguard Song arrived. Li Kui and Bao Xu each presented a severed head. When the commanders recognized the heads of Gao Keli and Zhang Jinren, they were all astonished and asked, “How did you obtain the heads of our enemies?” The two replied, “We killed a great many men. We meant to take those two alive, but our hands began to itch and we could not restrain ourselves, so we killed them on the spot.” Song Jiang said, “Now that we have the heads of our enemies, let us set them beneath the white banner and offer sacrifices facing the open sky to Generals Han and Peng.” Song Jiang wept once more, then lowered the white banner and rewarded Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun. Afterward he advanced his forces to the walls of Changzhou.

p.src: Now Privy Councillor Lü was panic-stricken inside the city. He consulted Jin Jie, Xu Ding, and the four commanders about a plan to repel Song Jiang. Having seen the havoc wrought by Li Kui and his companions, all the commanders trembled with fear and none dared go out to fight. Though he asked them several times, it was as if an arrow had sealed the wild goose’s beak or a hook had caught the fish by the gills: they remained silent, and no one dared answer. Privy Councillor Lü was vexed. When he sent men up the walls to look, Song Jiang’s forces had surrounded Changzhou on three sides and were all below the walls, beating drums, waving banners, shouting, and challenging the defenders to battle. Privy Councillor Lü ordered the commanders to take their respective posts atop the walls and defend them for the time being. After the commanders withdrew, Privy Councillor Lü sat alone in the rear hall, pondering without finding any plan. He summoned his closest attendants and trusted followers to confer, privately intending to abandon the city and flee. But that need not be told here.

p.src: Now the defending general Jin Jie returned home and said to his wife, Qin Yulan, “Vanguard Song has surrounded the city and is attacking it from three sides. We have little grain left in the city and cannot withstand a prolonged siege; if the city should fall, we shall all become ghosts beneath the sword.” Qin Yulan replied, “You have always cherished loyalty and filial devotion and wished to surrender. Moreover, you were formerly an official of the Song, and the court has never wronged you. Better to forsake evil and return to righteousness: capture Lü Shinang and present him to Vanguard Song. That would be the way to advance your fortunes.” Jin Jie said, “He now has four commanders under him, each with troops of his own. That scoundrel Xu Ding is also at odds with me and is one of Lü Shinang’s trusted intimates. I fear the affair may not succeed and will instead bring disaster upon us.” His wife said, “Secretly compose a sealed letter in the dead of night, fasten it to an arrow, and shoot it out of the city to inform Vanguard Song, so that you may coordinate within and without to take the city. p.src: The next day, Song Jiang pressed the attack on the city fiercely. Privy Councillor Lü gathered the officers to confer, and Jin Jie replied, “The walls of Changzhou are high and extensive. We should defend them, not meet the enemy in the field. Let the commanders hold their positions firmly until reinforcements arrive from Suzhou; only then should we unite our forces and give battle.” Privy Councillor Lü said, “Your words are entirely correct!” He assigned the commanders as follows: Ying Ming and Zhao Yi were to guard the eastern gate; Shen Bian and Fan Chou were to guard this gate; Jin Jie was to guard the western gate; and Xu Ding was to guard the southern gate. Once the assignments had been settled, each man led his troops to maintain a firm defense. That evening Jin Jie wrote a secret letter and fastened it to an arrow. When the night was deep and all was still, he went atop the wall and shot it down toward the scouts outside the western gate. A soldier picked up the arrow and hurriedly carried word back into the camp. The commanders of the western camp, Lu Zhishen the Tattooed Monk and Wu Song the Pilgrim, examined it and immediately sent the deputy commander Du Xing to carry it swiftly to the main camp by the northeastern gate. Song Jiang and Wu Yong were discussing affairs in the command tent by the light of bright candles. Du Xing presented Jin Jie’s secret letter. Song Jiang was overjoyed after reading it and at once issued orders that all three camps be informed.

p.src: He served a wicked court—deep cause for shame; yet dying for the right made fragrant even his bones upon the field. To become in later days Zhongshan's loyal ghost—how could that compare with dying in Fang La's ranks?

p.src: That day Commissioner Zhang and Commander Liu rewarded Jin Jie, then hacked the three rebels to pieces and displayed their severed heads to the public. They immediately sent men to Changzhou to reward the troops of the Song vanguard.

p.src: Now Song Jiang had his forces stationed at Changzhou. He sent Dai Zong to the armies of Vanguard Lu in Xuanzhou and Huzhou to carry an urgent message concerning the movement of troops. Meanwhile a scout rode in to report that Privy Councillor Lü had fled back to Wuxi County, joined forces with reinforcements from Suzhou, and was preparing to advance and meet them in battle. When Song Jiang heard this, he mustered cavalry and infantry, assigned ten principal and subordinate commanders a force of ten thousand, and sent them southward to meet the enemy. The ten commanders were Guan Sheng, Qin Ming, Zhu Tong, Li Ying, Lu Zhishen, Wu Song, Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun. Guan Sheng and the others took command of the vanguard troops and horses, bade farewell to Vanguard Song with their fellow commanders, and departed from the city.

p.src: Now Dai Zong gathered news of the armies advancing through Xuanzhou and Huzhou, then returned with Chai Jin to see Song Jiang. He reported that Deputy Vanguard Lu Junyi had taken Xuanzhou and had specially sent Lord Chai to announce the victory. Song Jiang was greatly delighted. When Chai Jin reached the prefectural offices, he paid his respects. Song Jiang offered him a welcoming cup, entered the rear hall with him, and sat down to ask for a full account of how Vanguard Lu had captured Xuanzhou. Chai Jin produced the official report and showed it to Song Jiang, then related the whole affair of the attack on Xuanzhou.

p.src: Fang La's Pacification Commissioner Jia Yuqing, who guarded Xuanzhou, had six regimental commanders under him, all natives of Shezhou or Muzhou. The six were Li Shao, Han Ming, Du Jingchen, Lu An, Pan Jun, and Cheng Shengzu. That day Jia Yuqing divided the six commanders into three forces and sent them out of the city to form battle lines. Vanguard Lu likewise divided his troops into three forces to meet them. In the center, Huyan Zhuo fought Li Shao, while Dong Ping engaged Han Ming. After ten bouts, Dong Ping killed Han Ming with two thrusts of his spears. Li Shao fled. The army in the center suffered a crushing defeat. On the left, Lin Chong fought Du Jingchen, while Suo Chao engaged Lu An. Lin Chong speared Du Jingchen to death with his serpent spear, and Suo Chao split Lu An with his axe. On the right, Zhang Qing fought Pan Jun, while Mu Hong engaged Cheng Shengzu. Zhang Qing knocked Pan Jun from his horse with a stone, and Li Zhong the Tiger-Slaying General chased him down and killed him. Cheng Shengzu abandoned his horse and fled back to the city. Four enemy commanders had now been defeated in succession that day, and the rebel troops withdrew into the city. Vanguard Lu at once drove his commanders forward to seize the city. But when they reached the gate, they were taken unawares by a great millstone hurled down from the wall, which killed one of our subordinate commanders. Arrows rained down from the walls, and every shaft was poisoned. Two more of our subordinate commanders were struck; they barely made it back to camp before both died. Seeing that three commanders had been lost, Vanguard Lu attacked the city throughout the night. The rebel commander guarding the east gate was lax, and thus Xuanzhou was taken. Li Shao was killed amid the fighting, while Jia Yuqing led the remnants of his defeated army away toward Huzhou. Zhishen was lost amid the battle lines, and no one knew where he had gone; the millstone had killed Zheng Tianshou, the Fair-Faced Gentleman; and the two struck by poisoned arrows were Cao Zheng, the Knife-Wielding Demon, and Wang Dingliu, the Lightning Goddess. When Song Jiang heard that three more of his brothers had been lost, he gave a great cry and suddenly fell to the ground. None knew the state of his inner organs, but they saw at once that his limbs would not move. Indeed: The blossom opens, only to be blown down by the wind; how can the bright moon endure being veiled by cloud and mist? What became of Song Jiang after he fainted, and whether his life was spared, will be told in the next chapter.
